game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
The premise seems interesting, but the game has some really annoying flaws that prevent me from enjoying it. Maybe it gets better later, but I couldn't tolerate it to get further.

The game constantly just wastes your time, it makes you wait through these long "chats" to catch "evidence". So you end up there, waiting, doing nothing, hoping that one day that chat ends and you can pick up the important pieces.

For some reason prevents you from changing your choices, so if you first think one option is right, then you can't choose another option later. For no other reason, than that the game says so.

It's often unclear as to what certain pieces of "evidence" mean, so you pick up a piece of text that the game tells you is important, and it turns out it's trying to save "wonderland" as a person's address which is ludicrous.

When there's conflicting information, the game sometimes just tells you "there's conflicting information somewhere, but I'm not going to tell you where ha ha good luck finding it", and sometimes it just tells you to throw dice and pick between two equally likely possibilities with no ability to change your opinion as you encounter more evidence later.

There's a tutorial fella that interrupts almost every single thing you do in the game for the first 15-30mins mostly just telling you useless things, or otherwise just annoying you, and there seems to be no chat log available for that.

Overall, I don't really get the point of most of this game.

review_text_raw:
This game could have been good, and the story is compelling to a certain extent. You can tell there is something that isn't being said that you can't find, and it makes it all the more important to find it. But thats where the fun stops, and where the frustration begins.

Probably the most aggrivating thing about this game is the inability to directly say what information you extract should mean. Instead you effectively hand over little quips of information to a conspiricy theorist and then wonder how that information is going to be used. Probably the biggest instance of this is when you are going to arrest a certain character, you get into a certain call. You learn that she is on the move, and has a hand gun. You submit that she has a gun and suddenly you basicaly called the fekin army down on her and she dies, when all evidence before then would suggest that going Riot-shields fer days would have been the correct move.

Also when handed "Contradicting evidence", often times the information isn't contradicting, but should have been able to be combined to paint something that would have been more conductive to profiling the person in question. Things like where the suspect lives now and previously, which both could be noted and later on used to help track down said person.

The lack of proper notes is, while not entirely nessisary for the set up of the game, probably a bad decision. Notes could have been used to snip articles with evidence that your unsure of how to use at the present moment and would have helped during the "Scrolling sections" disguised as Texts and calls. While you can scroll up during any moment of these, being able to hold out on certain information for a better time would have helped immensely.

So all in all, a great premise and the story works, execution worked about as well as alcohol and fire.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell was an enjoyable, but very flawed game. I struggle with recommending it to anybody, because I can't imagine a particular audience falling in love with it. Gamers looking for a great narrative may find Orwell's offerings lacking, as I have. Gamers who are fans of the works of George Orwell may get what they're looking for, but as a fan myself I find the game's vision lacking. George Orwell's works were a denouncement of totalitarianism, yet his most well-known fictional books were either set in the real world or clearly based on real events and people. Orwell the game instead opts to take place in the wonderful setting of "The Nation" in which "The Party" exercises total control in a fictional world.

While the setting certainly lacks creativity, I was pleased to see that the plot and characters of the game improved as time passed. Orwell places the player as a worker for a state surveillence system looking for the perpetrator of a series of terrorist bombings. The player is tasked with reading various articles, profiles, and personal conversations and sending this information to the authorities within The Nation's government. This sounds more interesting than it plays out, however. In the beginning I was given a suspect who was very clearly not the bomber. I resented my superior for being so brainless for assuming they were responsible. While this suspect inevitably had some connections with people who actually did know more about the bombings, I was frustrated that I had to investigate the suspect in the first place. The gameplay also lacks for imagination. While I enjoyed reading some of the articles and the suspect's internet profiles, conversations, and e-mails, the text that you upload is already pre-determined. It ultimately boils down to a scavenger hunt. There are some choices to make things interesting. Sometimes you will have to chose between two pieces of data to upload to the authorities, as there may be conflicting data. Sometimes this decision is a moral one, and others it's more based around what the player things is more accuracte information. There are even a few times where uploading too much information will lead to unforeseen consequences. Regardless, for the most part the gameplay is very linear and will ultimately turn off many gamers. The gameplay gets more interesting in the final chapter when the uploads you can make are limited and the pressure is heightened, yet this improvement comes too little, too late.

Orwell is a game I want to love and there are moments of quality within. The general conclusion to the story was pulled off fairly well and there are consequences for chocies that many probably would not have anticipated being held accountable for. The characters and their interactions amongst each other are far more engaging than the uncreative setting. I hope for the sequel the developers be more bold with their setting, their message, and ultimately make the gameplay more interesting for a wider audience.

The Orwell games are simply brilliant. No, seriously, there’s no hidden “but” here. If there ever was a series of games that I can recommend to literally everybody, it would be these two. Not because of their gameplay or their writing, though both of those are still good. No, the reason why I recommend you go out, buy and play these two games is because nothing I’ve seen elsewhere demonstrates the problems of government surveillance better than this.

In the first game, you’re put into the role of an agent tasked with finding the people responsible for a terrorist attack involving the detonation of an explosive at a public plaza. This all takes place in a fictional country called The Nation. The character you play as isn’t a citizen of The Nation though. Its government is outsourcing the surveillance of its people to external contractors who get paid to scour the internet and tap into phone conversations. Your job is to feed information back to a software called Orwell, which stores and processes all this data. You also have an advisor, who only gets to see the data that you feed into the software and they draw their own conclusions based on what information you feed them, which also determine certain future actions in the narrative. You can choose to omit information and sometimes you find conflicting or contradictory information where you have to choose, which of the two you want to pass along, since it doesn’t allow you to just collect both.

You get to violate the privacy of a number of citizens of the Nation and in the process have to figure out who’s behind the attacks. Naturally, everybody has a motive, since the government of the Nation isn’t too well regarded in certain spheres of its population. 

What fascinates me the most here is that both games obviously want to steer you into doing the right thing. And by “the right thing”, I mean to not simply rat out everybody and instead really take in the context of what people are saying. Every data chunk that you can collect in your database tells you what exactly is being extracted from it. So, if, say, a character is angry and says something metaphorically threatening or violent or if someone is generally impulsive, the data chunk reveals that Orwell and your advisor always take stuff like this 100% literally. There’s no room for nuanced interpretation or metaphor. It really makes you consider what information you’re willing to feed into the system and what’s better left where it is.

At first, I thought that this was fairly annoying, especially because it can also happen at times when you really have no other choice than to pick up that data chunk for the story to progress. But that too is part of the message that the game is sending. Government surveillance often lacks context and instead uses isolated details from which to conclude the bigger picture. Multiple times, your advisor draws conclusions and puts actions into motion against characters just as new information about them is coming to light, so the game constantly reminds you that these are supposed to be real people. They may lie to certain characters too and therefore lead you into the wrong direction. And forcing you to ignore that context at certain points even though you’re aware that it exists should tell you as a player something about government surveillance and maybe inform your opinion of it. The game also forces you to focus only on characters that the game lets you investigate. Now this is obviously a limitation of the game in and of itself because the developers can’t create tons of meaningless characters for you to investigate only for the lead to go nowhere. But it also once again comments on how government surveillance can sometimes turn a blind eye to the obvious by merely focusing on whatever is directly in front of it. 

The thing is though that at this point I have to mention that the actual gameplay is fairly simplistic and rudimentary. In essence it’s little more than a visual novel, since most of the time you’re just reading. There’s little in terms of flair going on, you’re literally just staring at a piece of software for most of it, browsing the web or reading along with phone calls and text messages. The second game thankfully features some voice acting for the phone conversations and podcasts, but you’re still mostly just reading stuff. I get that this isn’t everybody’s cup of tea and that many people don’t play games to simply sit there and read something, so the Orwell games won’t be for everybody. But I’d still urge you to try them out simply because of how effectively they convey their message. They’re also not that long, the first game takes around 5 hours to complete. Though there’s plenty of replay value to see how things might turn out otherwise if you made other decisions and maybe played as a blindly loyal character who doesn’t care whose lives he gets to ruin. So yeah, all in all, I definitely recommend the Orwell games.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I've always been one to read all of the books/letters/e-mails in games, but they rarely do more than build the world or give character backstory. I also tend to agonize over decisions in dialogue trees, worried that the "wrong" answer will cut me off from more interesting story lines. Orwell is a game that completely commits to reading and interpreting as the primary game mechanics. It succeeds at telling a satisfying story, even if it sometimes trips on the complexities of these mechanics as storytelling tools.

There are issues: The interface isn't as robust as you would hope. For instance, you can drag pictures of people from the Web into their profile, but only certain ones. At one point I found pictures of two new "persons of interest" on their corporation's website, but I couldn't drag their photos into their profiles. The game also runs into the issue that we have expectations of what can be done on the Internet. For instance, when you get the ability to break into someone's phone and can see where they've been, you expect that the addresses will tell you what is actually at those locations, but Orwell doesn't tell you this, you have to either remember or infer what is there.  

You can also get trapped when the story tries to funnel you to a certain plot point. In one part of the game there was nothing for me to do but to choose between two pieces of conflicting information: Which of two people organized a protest? The problem is that there was no way for me to make that call, it was pure he said/she said. I had a hunch, but it wasn't backed by any concrete information, and given what I had come to realize was the black-and-white nature of the Orwell system, I wanted to have something concrete before making this decision. Unfortunately, in order to progress the story I was forced to make the call based on nothing more than a hunch. 

And sometimes it seems like you need to make the wrong choice when one set of conflicting information would clearly open up a whole new tangent and the conflicting data wouldn't, so you choose the first even though you know the second is just as likely to be correct. For instance, at one point a character was accused of being gay, but there was conflicting information that he actually had a wife and kids. Of course, these two things don't conflict at all, there are plenty of gay people who have been in heterosexual relationships and even marriages. In fact, this character left his wife and children and the accusation that he was gay came many years later, so clearly one could argue that he left his wife and family BECAUSE he was gay. But in order to progress the story and open up profiles on the wife and learn more about that part of his life, I had to choose the wife data over the gay data. 

Sometimes the AI just breaks, especially that of your handler, Symes. For instance, one time I added the info that a certain character had a new girlfriend, that he wasn't with his old girlfriend, Juliet. Symes chimed in that he never knew that this character and Juliet were a couple, but I had put that information in both of their profiles a long time ago. And sometimes Symes is just clueless: At one point we discovered the name of a new character, one for whom we previously only knew her online handles, and he said something like "So she's been hiding her real name, eh?" Of course she was! Who always uses their real name for their online accounts?

It seems that there are probably multiple endings, but I only played it through once. There are no manual saves, so to get other endings you would have to play through the whole game again, which I'm not interested in doing. I wasn't entirely satisfied with my ending, but I still think that the journey was compelling and timely, probably more timely than the developers even realized when they started working on it. Orwell is a fascinating experience, especially if you are at all interested in our current information culture and the balance between government data gathering and personal privacy.

Bought it cause I'm into Orwell and dystopian stories and such. Was very disappointed. You click on a page and either look for the clickable blue text or waste your time and read it and get immersed like I did. To put it simply, boring. But I stuck with it and gave it a shot. What really grinds my gears is the yellow text. It is supposed to be "contradictory" statements, but is anything but.

For example, the first woman you investigate has two posts that "contradict" each other where in one post she calls another woman her best friend and in the other she gets mad at said woman. THAT. IS. NOT. CONTRADICTORY. IF ANYTHING, getting frustrated and having strained relationships with friends is extremely common. But you can only pick one making the story that she either "hates the woman" or "is her best friend" instead of the simple truth that she is her best friend AND they get into fights as can be explained later by the woman being off of her meds.

If you're someone who doesn't like this type of game, you won't enjoy it so don't buy it. If you do enjoy this type of game, you'll likely be disappointed like I was and won't enjoy it, so don't buy it. Not worth even at a sale.

review_text_raw: I really want this game to be good. The idea of being Big Brother fighting against freedom groups while they make comments about your injustice is fascinating. However, the game barely passes as a game and more of a click and listen to your boss speak. Only a few pieces of information are "conflicting," and once you decide on what conflicting data is correct, you can't undo your choice. Why would I not be able to update a database with new information? There are actually pieces of data that will replace older ones, so the mechanic is literally staring you in the face. Also, almost every piece of data you acquire results in your boss making some comment. A few are useful, such as him making an interesting connection. But have of them are "that's weird, huh." Or extremely stupid ones like "trouble in paradise, eh." The core game play loop is click on tab with red star, find blue highlights, drag them to the left, listen to boss be an idiot, repeat. If the game was left with the ability to select what text you believe is appropriate and then sent you on your own, it'd be much better. If you could assemble the reports and see the result, e.g., if a jury deemed your target guilty, then it'd be amazing. As it stands, its an amazing concept with terrible execution.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
TL;DR: If you want to be a pedantic bureaucrat, play "Papers, please" instead.


Long story:

This can be an exciting game if you're not one who likes nitpicking. However, if you do (which is maybe why you're drawn to it in the first place), you will pull some hairs out in rage and discontent.

The game focuses on monitoring an increasing set of data (news, websites, chat logs, phone calls etc) to look for leads in a specific case on which the game is built up. Whatever the game means is relevant will be highlighted, and you'll have the choice to either submit it to the investigators or ignore it. The info will also be rewritten, i.e. concentrated to what the game thinks it means.

This poses two problems - 1) the data YOU might think is highly relevant or more relevant isn't highlighted. And 2) the data you find may not be the data that will be submitted. For example, someone SUGGESTS to someone else that they do something. If you submit it, it's altered to say that the person PLANNED it. When talking about a crime that may or may not have occurred, this is a very important difference. Casually suggesting something and planning it is not the same. Everything you submit will be used by the police to decide which actions to take, so you might want to ignore that piece of info then.. if you can (explained further down).

Sometimes you find "contradicting info", and you can only pick one of the contradicting pieces (or ignore them altogether, of course). Sometimes these pieces of information don't contradict each other, but you still have to pick only one.

The game follows a story, and some key facts are needed in order to move it along. Once in a while you experience that the game doesn't progress, apparently because it won't continue until you've provided a key "fact" in the story. So you'll have to go through the stuff you ignored and guess which one the game wants you to submit before moving on. And yes, sometimes that includes incorrect information. Which causes rage quitting on my part, because the whole point of you making sure facts are provided is taken away.

The developers should have points for making a complex story and managing to implement this as a game - the way they have made it both simple, complex and engaging should be praised, as well as the psychological profiles of the suspects, showing how easily having inner access to their thoughts without having the proper context can lead to false conclusions. But the lack of preciseness and logical snafus in the interface makes what could have been an interesting take at the pros and cons of the surveillance society into a silly, semi-intellectual murder mystery for the masses.

review_text_raw:
[h1]A fun little game with a few annoyances.[/h1]
[i]Review correct as of episode 2[/i]


Orwell plays its premise on its sleeve, but that's not a bad thing. Orwell's a lovely modern take on the dystopian Orwellian society from 1984, where surveillance is king and social media reveals your darkest secrets. The ruling government of your fictional country; rather menacingly known as, 'The Party'; is toned down to a believable level, less thought police coming to take those whom merely forget the government's new lie; more observing and taking people who know more than they think for a quick chat... In a windowless cell...

You play a new agent to an experimental scheme, brought about by their version of the patriot act, who spys on its people to counter terrorist acts. Unfortunately, you've come at a bad time, there's been a dramatic terrorist bombing and you've got to find those reponsible. Luckily, deus ex machina, you've been directed to a person of interest whom happens to be very weakly linked to the terrorist/s. Better start investigating. 

Investigations are done by exploring a person's current and past life in detail and it's a fun little bit of gameplay. You simply open either a website or a report and the, "government's advanced computers", scan the page for anything it thinks relevant to the investigation. It's up to you to decide what to include in your report by dragging and dropping highlighted items onto said report. Sadly, Osmotic Studios has decided that you can't change anything you drag onto your report. Accidentally mistake a bit of text saying they live in Wonderland as information on their mental instability rather than what the game has decided, which is that they physically live in Wonderland? Well tough titties, you can't change that. 

At times the game does spice things up with multiple choice moments. Throughout the game, contradictory information will be presented to you and it's up to you to decide which is the correct bit of information. But! But! There isn't always an obvious answer! Which infuriates a few people. But it shouldn't. People who get frustrated are sadly missing the obvious answer the game's trying to present to you. The truth doesn't matter. You are the truth. What you decide can and will be the truth. You pick the option which suits your needs, think person A is a dissdent to 'The Party'? Then the correct answer is that the man is a dissdent. No matter what contradictory information you see. This is the beauty of Orwell and this is were the game really shines. Sometimes though these options are forced. Two bits of information are in fact the same piece of information just it's presented in a way to force a choice, when in reality you could easily push both those pieces in a well worded report.

While the gameplay is enjoyable, where Orwell really shines is in it's narrative. The characters you are investigating are nicely fleshed out and you can get a real sense of who that person is and that's an important factor in a game like this. No matter how good a story you have, if the people you are investigating are dull or unbelievable it could really ruin a game like this, gladly I can say this hasn't happened. While it is rather short it has a nice progression and you can feel the underlying sense a deeper plot and the frustrating feeling of grasping at the strings of truth. A feeling further emphasised by the episodic nature of the game, gladly the timeframe is rather short and the feeling is rather than them having a product that isn't complete, they're trying to tailor the story from the fans suggestions and mood.

There weren't many things I disliked about Orwell. My biggest gripe is almost a personal choice, I've already mentioned a few smaller issues already such as forced choices and the fact information placed into the report cannot be edited, but I think Orwell misses a beat when it comes to power of the government. It wants to present a Orwellian society for the modern day and tries to do this by suggesting your powers and the government's powers are legally limited at certain moments. This is personally the opposite way I wish they had gone. For starters modern goverments have incredible powers just have a gander at the Patriot Act (US),  the 2000/2006 terrorism act (GB), and états d'urgence - constitution of 1958 (Fr). I wish Orwell had taken this and gone further, showing a government whose powers were even more unfettered.

In summation I rather like Orwell and it's a game I can very heartily recommend to anyone who would like a nice story driven narrative, and can get through the rather lengthy bits of text one has to read. There are some personal gripes I have with the story but overall nothing that you would really be a deal breaker.

Luckily, deus ex machina, you've been directed to a person of interest whom happens to be very weakly linked to the terrorist/s. Better start investigating. Investigations are done by exploring a person's current and past life in detail and it's a fun little bit of gameplay. You simply open either a website or a report and the, "government's advanced computers", scan the page for anything it thinks relevant to the investigation. It's up to you to decide what to include in your report by dragging and dropping highlighted items onto said report. Sadly, Osmotic Studios has decided that you can't change anything you drag onto your report. Accidentally mistake a bit of text saying they live in Wonderland as information on their mental instability rather than what the game has decided, which is that they physically live in Wonderland? Well tough titties, you can't change that. At times the game does spice things up with multiple choice moments. Throughout the game, contradictory information will be presented to you and it's up to you to decide which is the correct bit of information. But! But! There isn't always an obvious answer! Which infuriates a few people. But it shouldn't. People who get frustrated are sadly missing the obvious answer the game's trying to present to you. The truth doesn't matter. You are the truth. What you decide can and will be the truth. You pick the option which suits your needs, think person A is a dissdent to 'The Party'? Then the correct answer is that the man is a dissdent. No matter what contradictory information you see. This is the beauty of Orwell and this is were the game really shines. Sometimes though these options are forced. Two bits of information are in fact the same piece of information just it's presented in a way to force a choice, when in reality you could easily push both those pieces in a well worded report. While the gameplay is enjoyable, where Orwell really shines is in it's narrative. The characters you are investigating are nicely fleshed out and you can get a real sense of who that person is and that's an important factor in a game like this. No matter how good a story you have, if the people you are investigating are dull or unbelievable it could really ruin a game like this, gladly I can say this hasn't happened. While it is rather short it has a nice progression and you can feel the underlying sense a deeper plot and the frustrating feeling of grasping at the strings of truth. A feeling further emphasised by the episodic nature of the game, gladly the timeframe is rather short and the feeling is rather than them having a product that isn't complete, they're trying to tailor the story from the fans suggestions and mood. There weren't many things I disliked about Orwell. My biggest gripe is almost a personal choice, I've already mentioned a few smaller issues already such as forced choices and the fact information placed into the report cannot be edited, but I think Orwell misses a beat when it comes to power of the government. It wants to present a Orwellian society for the modern day and tries to do this by suggesting your powers and the government's powers are legally limited at certain moments. This is personally the opposite way I wish they had gone. For starters modern goverments have incredible powers just have a gander at the Patriot Act (US), the 2000/2006 terrorism act (GB), and états d'urgence - constitution of 1958 (Fr). I wish Orwell had taken this and gone further, showing a government whose powers were even more unfettered. In summation I rather like Orwell and it's a game I can very heartily recommend to anyone who would like a nice story driven narrative, and can get through the rather lengthy bits of text one has to read. There are some personal gripes I have with the story but overall nothing that you would really be a deal breaker.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1] A very enjoyable game with hidden depth, despite the very simple game mechanics. [/h1]

You investigate persons of interest in a bombing (i.e read a whole bunch and invade peoples' privacy) through their online information and electronic devices via Orwell, The Nations new secret surveilence system. The people and ways you can investigate are not all immediately available, you unlock more options and imformation based on the data you upload and where you are in the story. The gameplay ultimately boils down to drag-and-droping the datachunks (that the game hightlights) that you think are relevent, into Orwell.

While on the surface the game may seem not very challenging or lacking in replayability as some claim, there are subtleties that make Orwell really great.

Such as the fact that you, as the investigator, are the only person who will see the [b] context [/b] of the data you're uploading. Mild episode 1 spoiler: [spoiler] See a woman joking with her boyfriend that she stole his credit card (which she uses to buy a bottle of wine), which he seems mildly annoyed by but seemingly fine with? Upload that into Orwell and all your superiors know is that she "stole a credit card". [/spoiler] Whether or not you think reporting that is morally right or not, it does have an effect on how things turn out for her.
There are several times such as this when the information you can upload is damning, incomplete or inaccurate simply because the datachunk lacks context. There are times when you can use this to your advantage, if say you want to frame someone winkwink.

There are also times where you will encounter "conflicting data chunks", where you have the choice of which one (sometimes if any) you wish to upload. These choices often lead to a person or circumstance being viewed in an entirely different manner. Sometimes it is the drastic difference between someone being seen as a terrorist or an innocent.
This is why it's very important to look very carefully at what a datachunk is really uploading to Orwell and remember you needn't and perhaps shouldn't upload everything.

Overall this game puts you into a position where you have to make a lot of moral decisions around privacy, relevancy, and generally be the judge of everyone you investigate. Your choices/ethics directly and indirectly influence the fate of all the characters you meet.

A brief note on replayability: I found there to be plenty of reasons to replay the game; be it for achievement hunting, because you messed up a lot the first time around (like me ^-^'), or just to see how everything pans out if you'd played differently. As of writing I have 11.3 hours on record and I still intend to play it further as I don't feel remotely done yet.
How much time you'll get out of it depends a lot on your playstyle and whether you're a completionist or someone who blitzes through games and doesn't bother with a replay.
The average time to finish your first run through seems to be around 4 or 5 hours for most people.

tldr: Tbh as long as you like detective and/or story-driven games, I whole-heartedly recommend Orwell. While I got it on sale, since playing I would totally pay full price.

P.S Try the demo because if you get to the end of it and feel the overwelming need to keep playing, you'll enjoy the full game.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Intresting premise,  poor execution. In the attempt to create stakes for the players decision, Orwell goes out of it's way to obfuscate or even fail to present clarfying information until after the decision is made. It also prevents refinement of past data with new context. Being forced to compete in the 20 meter jump to conclusions in order to find the context you needed to make that conclusion is beyond obxnoxious. This is made worse by there being minimal clarity to what the data you've supplied will be intreperted as, and that intreptation is final with little abitliy to recontextualize. 

This of course undermines any moral arguement the game attempts to present or have you consider. Over surveillance, the effect of technology on the governments ability to monitor it's citizens and so forth are good topics to explore. However demonstarting the conquences by forcing the player to pick up the idiot ball does no one any favours.  

The concept is good, if you can deal with being forced to make uncontextualized leaps of judgement you might enjoy the game. But the inability to use good inquirial practices like preserving and rexamining conflicting data in light of new evidence kills the game for me.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This game is a dishonest indictment against current surveilance and privacy ethics. It tries to force you into an unethical position so that it can pull off a "gotcha" moment for emotional impact and cheap pedantic morals. You play the nameless analyst that feeds the State with information about people trying to prevent crimes through surveilance of private communications and crossreference of public sources. So far so good. The problems start when the writers remove player agency and predestine outcomes. This happens in two ways.

1) The game uses a system of "conflicting data chunks" which are SUPPOSEDLY contradictory information pieces and you have to judge which is the correct one. Only they aren't. Say that you ram a car in a crossroad in rage. And you do it because you know that this car is going to kill your parents in the next stop. Are these contradictory? Well for this game they are. And you get different outcomes if you select one or the other to "push" to your supervisor. This is called lazy writing and removes player agency. Moving on...

2) You work a narrative case to your best judgement and then the game robs you of an outcome that is as obvious as a billboard on a busy highway. Say that you have a classic crime procedural where the detective is trying to break a suspect. Imagine the detective knows that the suspect is ethical and peaceful and that there is going to be a murder unless the suspect gives up a criminal acquaintance. The expected narrative would be to appeal to humanity and have a reasonable resolution. But no. The game, having known that you did not went for the "cog in the machine" trope, for cheap emo guilt trips, pulls a gotcha and just blows the murder on your face saying you "failed".

At the time of writing this review there is an article in Kotaku about "ludo-narrative dissonance", i.e. how gameplay conflicts with narrative. (link: https://kotaku.com/the-bioshock-problem-when-gameplay-and-narrative-clash-1847698124). This, sometimes can be a good thing as it might shed light into serious ethical conundrums for the player. 
Here the attempt fails because the writers and designers went pedantic and decided to rob the players of even the off chance to experience a story where things would plausibly move in a more nuanced direction than the beat to death pseudo-dilemma "bad state vs bad people" and "security vs freedom". 

Instead of exploring the grey area of these ethics they threw every stereotype in the book to the player and plain and simple punished them when they did not conform to their teenage black and white mentality. 

It's a pity, the review is coming late, but don't bother...

review_text_raw:
This game is close to being unique (it's a bit Hacknet/Uplink but with a wonderfully minimal UI and no typing (yet), it also reminds me of a 90s game called Floor 13 which was about conducting political espionage), is interesting and smart, and is just overall fun to play. If you want to embroil yourself in convicting people of crimes based on things they've basically written on Facebook then go for it.

Negatives: The choices, I suspect, will only ever be binary. The fact that the game flags up conflicting data-chunks **even thought you've only seen the first one of the two** works against the immersion slightly.

But overall I'd wholeheartedly recommend this to anyone who wants to play a game about heavy-handed surveillance culture where anything anyone does works against them.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[b]tl;dr:[/b] The description doesn't make clear that this is a visual novel. Don't expect much decision making, or even actual deduction--[i]Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You[/i] holds your hand throughout the experience. If you can forgive that, and stomach the occasionally doubleplusungood prose, you'll have a decent (if predictable) exploration of surveillance. Modestly recommended; only buy during sales.

-

It's the World Of Tomorrow™, and an enigmatic nation known only as, well, The Nation is preparing the implementation of an as of yet unannounced surveillance program. With the Orwell AI on your side, you are tasked with finding the culprit of a terrorist attack, so that the government can prove the efficacy of the program and rally the support of the public. But things are not as they seem, and what was supposed to be a simple case quickly spirals out of control.

Actual gameplay, if it can be called that, mostly consists of diving into the digital lives of target persons. Now and then, the AI will highlight processable pieces of information, which are known as datachunks. If you feed a datachunk to the system, it will be sent to a government advisor on the other end of the line, who can then use the evidence to justify an arrest, call in a special ops team, et cetera. Because the advisor only gets to see those datachunks that you choose to process, he can't really read the information in its proper context, allowing you to paint a misleading picture through selectivity. By (ab)using this indirect influence, you can steer the turn of events into your preferred direction.

The idea sounds interesting enough on paper, and admittedly, it sometimes is--when the game is at its best, your choices really [i]do[/i] feel as if they matter. More often than not, though, you just go down a funnel, with your advisor telling you what to do for every step of the way. Events are supposed to happen in real-time, but are actually tied to your storyline progress; after something significant has happened, events will usually grind to a halt until you've passed some checkpoint. This implementation strips the concept of much of its strength, and it would be nice if Osmotic Studios had been a tad bit more honest about this. Indeed, I went in with a much more sandboxy expectation. Buyer, beware: [i]Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You[/i] is a glorified visual novel, with no real interaction beyond some scripted points of divergence. I don't think that is necessarily a bad thing. I [i]do[/i] think it is important to know.

Another thing that cheapens the experience is the implausible interface of the AI. From time to time, you will encounter two contradictory datachunks, but instead of doing the sensible thing (uploading them both for later review), the AI will [i]force[/i] you to make a choice, even if you don't have nearly enough context to do so informedly. For some reason, these uploads can't be reversed if you find better information down the road. Even more questionably, the AI can somehow [i]know[/i] that a certain datachunk will contradict with another, even if the contradicting datachunk hasn't been found yet! I understand that these things are necessary for gameplay purposes--calling the shots in solving contradictions is one of the key ways to manipulate your advisor--but they really do shatter one's immersion.

So far, I have been pretty negative about this game, so you might be wondering why I still recommend it. The reason is quite simple: the story, is well worth experiencing. Characters feel like real, actual people who could be living next door, not like empty robots who are just there to advance the plot. And it is the very lack of meaningful choice that allowed the writers to go this far: most games are wide but shallow, [i]Orwell[/i] is narrow but deep. Granted, the attempts to make the player question their own morality mostly fall flat (contrary to what the reviewer consensus seems to be, good and evil are clear from the start), and the social commentary that permeates the writing has a distinct feeling of 'heard it all before'. There is also an overreliance on deus ex machina, particularly near the end of the story. But the characters and their various interactions are captivating enough to make you genuinely care about their fates. You might even find yourself on the edge of your seat, even though you never get to see the action directly. In my opinion, that more than makes up for the cheap plot devices, as well as the [i]very[/i] variable quality of the prose. The many references to George Orwell's [i]Nineteen Eighty-Four[/i] add to the charm.

In short, [i]Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You[/i] is a mediocre game, but with a respectable narrative. As long as you keep your expectations in check, it will certainly provide an afternoon of entertainment.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1] "For The Nation, for the security of the citizens, for their safety, I shall be the investigator. The one who shall observe and... eliminate." [/h1]

What is in this mysterious name: Orwell? A good plot? Realism and coherence? A branching storyline? Memorable characters? Plot twists? Perhaps, all of the mentioned and a lot more? Yes - all of the mentioned and A LOT more. This game is a very interesting game in which you'll act as an investigator working for a governmental project called "Orwell." With the help of this mass surveillance software/tool, you will be tracking and evaluating various people to identify potential "threats" to The Nation. The evaluation process includes analyzing social media accounts of the people evaluated, their chat histories, emails, phone calls, personal devices, and etc. Basically anything, which they deemed a part of their "private" life. 

What I really liked about this game is its attention to detail. On the first look, the game's storyline contains lots of unnecessary snippets of information, which might be regarded as useless by the inattentive player. However, those little details and discrepancies form a larger picture which reveals a major plot twist that takes place somewhere in the ending episodes. The plot twist itself [spoiler], which was about Juliet being the imposter instead of the suspected Harrison,[/spoiler]did make sense after some other playthroughs (accomplishing all the achievements and endings) as I've paid a lot of attention to those little details in the game. [spoiler]For me, the hint provided by Symes about Juliet's favorite book (The Mockingbird)and Harrison's lost phone seemed like the ones which can directly lead you towards the "Juliet is the true imposter" conclusion. [/spoiler]Well, the game proved to me that no story can be regarded as completely explored without the consideration of all the small details. A lesson well learnt.

As much as I liked this game, there are still things that can be improved. For instance, adding a setting for an accelerated playthrough, because DAMN, some of the calls take more than 10 minutes to finish and are unskippable. Going through the game again becomes a real pain without this feature. I understand that some events happen during phone calls (which is probably why you can't accelerate them), but as a person who finished the main plot multiple times, I don't bother to read all the stuff again. Besides, I think players decide beforehand their choices, so adding the accelerated playthrough won't hurt the experience much (it is wise to lock it until the game is completed for the first time). There were some spelling (Episode 3; objective; "motiviation") and grammar mistakes, but those are minor issues. Apart from these, there aren't much things which I'd want to be added to this game.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This is not a game. It's more like a fancy choose your own adventure book. There is a limited number of ways that the story completes, and other than a few important decision points your actions have little consequence to how the story plays out. See the  Wikipedia page if you want to know the story before hand.  

I did not enjoy this experience, i did not find it fun, and here are my main complaints:

1) You spend all of your  time sifting through emails and texts looking for important information or data chunks. This is not a challenge because the information is highlighted for you. To make matters  even dumber, the specific emails, texts, etc are marked with an icon to show you which ones have the important information you need to act on.

2) The important decision points in the game are also highlighted in bright yellow as conflicting data chunks. You have to choose which one Orwell (the computer) will consider as fact. Often times you have to do this without any way of knowing the actual truth, but the implications of the choices are always glaringly obvious. 

3) There are data chunks that have to be given to Orwell for the story to progress, even if you don't  want to provide it. This is the one thing the ruined the experience for me, and made it obvious that the program is leading you by the nose and you have no real control. I get it. You can't read a book from the middle out, and in a "game" that is basically just a click-through-story you have to proceed in the order the author intends. All the important information has to be in place for the story to make sense. 

Lastly, and this is a minor quibble, but I also take issue with the name of this "game". Orwell is a stupidly ironic name. George Orwell was an opponent of totalitarianism, not it's champion. Perhaps a better literary subject to steal would have been Colossus (Dennis Feltham Jones). At least that Colossus was a computer.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1] George Orwell rolls in his grave [/h1]

Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You is an interactive novel exploring the increasingly popular notion that G. Orwell’s iconic “1984” ended up being a guideline for running a country, rather than a warning to its citizens. True to dystopian tones of its inspiration, the title opens up with a bombing attack on a public plaza. Several people were killed, perpetrators are unknown and public is in an uproar. This where you come in, as hand-picked investigator you will use the latest marvel of civil protection technology – Orwell, to solve the case. Orwell “the first and the last line of defence against terrorism” is a powerful software capable of accessing everything connected to the internet. Once a person is authorised by higher-ups for investigation, you are to upload any useful chunks of data into the software and Orwell will process them, granting you access to further information on the target. Person of interest has their phone number on their social media page? Now you can listen to their calls. An e-mail address published on their company’s website? Let’s take a peek inside. Is that a PC id number? You know the drill by now.

[b] Big brother stays vigilant [/b]
With power of Orwell at your fingertips, the player becomes breach of privacy incarnate, yet the decision whether to upload something or not is yours to make. At times you will have conflicting data, that may mislead the authorities acting upon your investigation, while certain details can be ignored altogether. On the other hand, there are also key data chunks that have to be uploaded in order to progress the story and, especially at early stages, there are not a lot of choices to make. Orwell is counterintuitive at first and software’s interpretation of data provided is downright puzzling at times. You better adapt to your new role quickly, as at certain junctions your choices will have an impact at the rest of the story.

It might have drawn your attention that I have addressed the title in question as an “interactive novel”, rather than a game. This is primarily due to the fact that aforementioned limited choice of data chunks thrown into the system is as far as gameplay goes. Alas, it is much easier to regard Orwell as a book, with webpages being equivalent of descriptions and eavesdropped calls and chats being the dialogues. Your investigation quickly unveils a hint of deeply-rooted conspiracy being at work and bombing is but a beginning of something much bigger. Plot divided into 5 chapters thickens quickly and while the general direction of the story is set in stone, your choices can greatly alter fate of certain characters and the ending is yours to twist.

[b] Blessed be the mind too small to question [/b]
Orwell is rather straight-forward with its thought-provoking intent. While the title’s plot unveils in delightfully ambiguous “The Nation”, it doesn’t take a particularly big leap of logic to start drawing parallels. Especially with themes of invigilation, media manipulation and a classic question of “whether the ends justify the means”. As with most of such questions and ideas, Orwell will be whatever you choose to make of it. It won’t be long though, as the title takes roughly 5 hours to complete, making it possible to finish Orwell in a single sitting. That said, the story is divided into coherent chapters of similar length, highlighted by the game as a good moment for a break, should you need one. Orwell is commendable for finding multiple sensible ways to underline impending conclusion of a plot thread, while staying reasonable from in-universe perspective.

Another facet of Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You, deserving a separate mention is the art style of the game. Admittedly, the opening cutscene fells remarkably clunky but everything past this very beginning is static images, allowing the style to truly shine. Every picture is built from colourful polygons giving the illustrations believable, yet somewhat obscured, feel to it. Much like the setting of the story, the visuals are deliberately vague, leaving making the parallels up to the player. 

When approached as a book, Orwell makes for enjoyable read with a highly unorthodox mode of delivery. I can easily recommend it to every fan of criminal thriller and political fiction as you should find yourself right at home. If one were to approach the title as a game though, there is very little to speak of. Should you also happen to be the type to skip dialogues in games as a habit, you should probably avoid Orwell like a plague.

P.S. Once you exit Orwell, you are greeted by advertisement of a sequel - Orwell: Ignorance is Strength. Fear not though, Keeping an Eye On You provides a complete storyline, no “to be continued” ending attached.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
What is Orwell ?

Orwell is a game that has managed to make me fully immersed into it, which is something rare, whenever a game makes me Immersed, it automatically makes that game good for me. In concept orwell introduces you into a terrorist situation and you are an hired investigator who must use this new tool called "Orwell" to bring justice to the people involved in this specific situation, the gameplay is very simple, its just clicking and dragging stuff on screen but I'd rather play this and be immersed than play the latest AAA release and fall asleep just 2 hours in, what makes Orwell special is that its a game that every single choice matter, nothing is black and white, for every stuff you do during your investigation, the special traits the supposed terrorist have that you highlight on their profile, to the locations they visited, their personal lives and the people they have a relationship with, all the occurrences that happen during the 5 days the game takes place on, whenever you finish one of the five chapters aka complete a day of investigations theres a lot of consequences, good or not based on what you decided to highlight, since Orwell itself as a program has a imbued browser system and a profile you have to search every corner for information and make sure that youre putting the correct person in jail, theres contradicting information, I for example failed hard on the second day of investigations, I sent the police to the wrong location and because of that a bomb exploded in a public area, killing innocents, something I could prevent and by the end of the game, no matter what you do, we both will always get different endings since theres so many variables at stake and Orwell is such a detailed and immersive game, it makes every decision count. Another thing to add is that the game plays into hard topics that are relevant to our current times and the game does it in such smart way, its not just another pretentious game, its a smart, well-done game. 

Besides the concept Orwell presents a nice soundtrack and a great sense of style, you will always be looking into this program for most of the time but the game uses this environment to show its great artistic design and despite the gameplay being overly simple with the complex way your decisions are taken into consideration, the immersion the game pulls you into and the very interesting way that this game story which Imo was really well done develops, it just becomes a seamless experience, it took me 5 hours to finish and I would gladly replay it again and this time correcting the mistakes I did on my previous playthrough, I think that Orwell is simple an indie masterpiece, it executes its concept with class, add interesting takes into the whole cybersecurity concept and has a simple but engaging gameplay, In my opinion if you want to try something different that stays with you then this game is a must-play, a very memorable and original game.
